A content delivery network is a system of computers spread across many cities and countries that work together to deliver web pages, videos, and images faster. Every website keeps its original, master copy of files on a single machine called the origin server, which is the main computer where content is first stored. Sending every visitor's request all the way to that one origin server would be slow, especially for people far away. To fix this, copies of the content get stored on many smaller computers positioned closer to where people actually are; each of these nearby computers is called an edge location because it sits at the edge of the network, near the audience rather than at the center. When someone requests a page, the nearby edge location checks whether it already has a saved copy. If it does, that success is called a cache hit, meaning the content was delivered instantly from nearby storage instead of being fetched from far away. Think of it like a chain of neighborhood libraries that each keep popular books on hand, so readers do not need to travel to one central library every time they want something to read. Only when a book is missing locally does the request travel back to the central branch. This arrangement makes websites load faster, reduces strain on the origin server, and keeps things working even when traffic spikes suddenly in one region.

| Term | Plain meaning | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| Origin server | The main computer holding the original files | It is the ultimate source everything else copies from |
| Edge location | A smaller computer near end users that stores copies | It shortens the distance content has to travel |
| Cache hit | A request answered from a nearby saved copy | It means faster loading and less work for the origin server |
| Content delivery network | The whole network of connected edge locations | It keeps websites fast and reliable worldwide |
